channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: MIA Watchlist: Track whether the US-Iran war widens and Brent breaks USD 110, whether Washington extends its Section 301 template beyond Brazil, the October EU-China rare-earth flashpoint, and which German car plants close or pass to Chinese owners.
item.description:
• Hormuz and oil: whether US strikes near Tehran and Iran's attacks on Gulf states widen into a regional war, and whether Brent breaks Goldman's USD 110 case as OECD reserves draw down.
  • Section 301 tariffs: whether Washington extends the Brazil template to other partners, Brazil's retaliation and WTO filing, and the vote path for the 100% Russian-energy tariff bill on China and India.
  • EU-China October flashpoint: the expiry of the temporary rare-earth arrangement and whether the EU crisis task force secures alternative critical-mineral supply.
  • European chemical base: the EU Methane Regulation's January 2027 hit to refinery runs, Japan's naphtha-reserve decision, and any further capacity closures after Descalzi's "20% closed" warning.
  • German autos: which plants close or pass to Chinese owners, and the 17 July Franco-German declarations on protecting European industry.

item.title: The US and China head for a September summit to review compliance rather than new deals, with Washington calling China's truce performance "not perfect" but avoiding action, as the EU launched a China consultation mechanism and a crisis task force.
item.description:
The superpower relationship is being deliberately stabilised. US Trade Representative Greer said the September meeting will "take stock of results" on the Busan truce — rare-earth suspensions, US soybean purchases, retaliatory-tariff rollbacks and fentanyl cooperation — while conceding China's compliance is "not perfect". Reporting suggests Trump's team believes China is violating the deal but is reluctant to act, unwilling to jeopardise a planned Xi state visit or reopen a trade war. The EU is playing a more defensive game: it launched a China-EU consultation mechanism covering trade balance, export controls, IP and WTO reform, while separately standing up an emergency task force to prepare for a possible October trade clash when a temporary rare-earth arrangement expires. Brussels is pressing Beijing to curb export pressure in mechanical engineering, autos and chemicals in exchange for flexibility on EV duties.

Industry Impact

The EU's explicit demand that China curb export pressure in chemicals makes this directly relevant: European chemical producers are named collateral in the deficit dispute, and the October rare-earth expiry is a concrete risk date. A managed US-China truce reduces near-term tail risk, but the underlying rivalry keeps supply-chain fragmentation on the agenda. For ACS producers, the practical signal is to track the October EU-China flashpoint and the September US-China summit as the two dates most likely to reset chemical trade conditions in H2.

Commercial Times | Chinatimes.com | People's Daily Online | Handelsblatt | Global Times

item.title: More than 870 wildfires are burning across Canada, pushing hazardous smoke into the US where New York opened mask-distribution sites, while the Canadian Red Cross launched an Ottawa Floods Appeal after an extreme-weather event on 1 July.
item.description:
The physical-risk theme recurs, this time centred on North America. Ontario alone has 177 active blazes among more than 870 nationwide, and by the evening of 16 July orange-level air-quality warnings covered Southern Ontario and the Greater Toronto Area, briefly making Toronto's air among the worst of any major city. The smoke crossed into the US, prompting New York's governor and city mayor to direct residents to free mask sites, with medical manufacturers pressing for US-made N95s. Simultaneously, the Ottawa region is still recovering from 1 July flooding severe enough to trigger a Red Cross appeal for immediate relief and longer-term resilience work. As in the last alert's China and Russia floods, the pattern is the same: climate disruption is now a recurring operating condition for industry and logistics, not an occasional event.

Industry Impact

Wildfire smoke and flooding disrupt construction and outdoor industrial activity — the demand base for many coatings and sealants — and can interrupt logistics and plant operations across affected regions. Recurring air-quality emergencies also raise worker-safety and operating-cost considerations for facilities in exposed areas. The takeaway for ACS producers is to build climate-resilience into North American logistics and site planning, with contingencies for smoke- and flood-driven disruption that are now predictable enough to plan against.

The Globe and Mail | AP | Financial Post

item.title: Italy's lower house approved an electoral overhaul that hands the winning coalition a seat bonus, strengthening Meloni before 2027, while France's field takes shape as Le Pen confirms a fourth Élysée bid and ex-PM Cazeneuve semi-declares.
item.description:
Two of the EU's largest economies are setting the terms of their next elections. In Italy, Meloni overcame coalition infighting to pass an electoral-reform bill 217–152, moving toward a proportional system with a majority bonus designed to blunt a newly united centre-left and Five Star opposition; the bill now goes to the Senate. In France, the 2027 contest is crowding early: Marine Le Pen has confirmed a fourth run despite an ineligibility ruling over embezzlement, unsettling a business community that had prepared for the more pro-European Jordan Bardella; former PM Bernard Cazeneuve has semi-declared as a left-republican outside the Socialist primary; and even ECB President Lagarde is engaging visibly in the campaign while denying she is a candidate. Elon Musk's public endorsement of Le Pen has added an external wildcard the RN says it is "not bound" by.

Industry Impact

Neither election is imminent, but both shape the medium-term policy backdrop for European industry — energy costs, industrial subsidies, EU cohesion and trade posture that determine whether chemical and manufacturing production stays competitive in Europe. A stronger Meloni majority and a Le Pen-inflected French race both point toward more nationalist industrial and trade policy. For ACS producers, the signal is planning-level: build political-risk scenarios for 2027 into European footprint and investment decisions rather than treating the regulatory environment as fixed.

Financial Times | Bloomberg | Handelsblatt | Les Echos | Suddeutsche Zeitung

item.title: Modi ordered ministries to identify 100-plus import categories — including chemicals, fertilizers and semiconductors — for domestic substitution, approved a INR 1.27tn Semicon 2.0, and saw the India-UK CETA take effect as an EU pact nears.
item.description:
India is pursuing resilience on two tracks at once: substitute imports and lock in preferential trade. Facing geopolitical risk and rupee pressure, Modi's office told ministries to target high-import goods — electronics, chemicals, key drugs, fertilizers, semiconductors, autos and machinery — with subsidies and incentives to scale local production. Semicon 2.0's INR 1.27tn outlay backs chip design, manufacturing and packaging. In parallel, the India-UK CETA entered force on 15 July, cutting tariffs on premium drinks (Scotch duty from 150% toward 40% by year ten), and Commerce Minister Goyal said an India-EU FTA will be signed by end-2026 for Q1 2027 entry, with a third India-EU Trade and Technology Council adding cooperation on AI, semiconductors and clean tech. The through-line is a bid to make India both less import-dependent and more deeply tied into Western supply chains.

Industry Impact

India's import-substitution drive explicitly names chemicals and fertilizers, so it is directly relevant: it points to rising domestic chemical capacity and potential new competition, but also to demand for technology, coatings and adhesives as manufacturing scales. The trade pacts open a large, growing market for ACS producers with EU or UK footprints. Watch India's product-substitution list for chemical categories, and weigh whether to serve the market through local production versus preferential-tariff exports once the EU FTA lands.

The Economic Times | Business Standard | The Economic Times | Business Standard | Vietnam News.Net

item.title: High-end manufacturing, the digital economy and services drove over 40% of China's H1 growth, and the World AI Conference opened in Shanghai with Xi's keynote as NVIDIA pulled four Japanese industrial giants into its physical-AI coalition.
item.description:
The strategy behind China's cooling headline growth comes into focus here. Preliminary data show high-tech manufacturing value-added up 13.3% in H1, with AI-linked segments — smart equipment, integrated circuits — growing above 30% and electronics and communications equipment output up 17%. Beijing is answering weak domestic demand by doubling down on the advanced-manufacturing engine rather than stimulating consumption. The 2026 World AI Conference (17–20 July) is the showcase: China's core AI industry topped CNY 1.2tn in 2025 across 6,200-plus firms, and Xi is using the platform to set out China's AI-governance positions. The competitive signal for the West is NVIDIA's parallel move — Fujitsu, Fanuc, Kawasaki and Yaskawa, joined by Hitachi, NEC, Komatsu and Kubota, are entering its Cosmos Coalition to accelerate factory robotics and physical AI, a Japan-anchored counterweight in the same race.

Industry Impact

The physical-AI and robotics build-out is a medium-term demand driver for ACS — electronics assembly, semiconductor packaging and robotics all use specialised adhesives, coatings and encapsulants. China's shift toward high-end manufacturing keeps its industrial materials demand growing even as construction-linked demand softens. But it also means faster Chinese self-sufficiency in advanced materials, a competitive threat over time. Position for AI-manufacturing-linked material demand while tracking how quickly Chinese suppliers close the specialty-chemical gap.

China Economic Net | China Daily | Chinatimes.com | China Daily | China Economic Net

item.title: Merz and Macron opened a two-day retreat near Cologne pledging to strengthen Europe's military, industrial and technological power, with joint declarations due 17 July and an effort to salvage elements of the stalled FCAS fighter project.
item.description:
After a bruising year between the EU's two largest economies, the retreat is pitched as consolidation rather than relaunch — building on last year's Toulon agreements. The agenda is deliberately broad: economic, energy, security and defence policy, plus Ukraine, the Middle East, space, AI, quantum, trade and the protection of European industry. The hard test is industrial cooperation. The two governments are trying to move past the collapse of the SCAF/FCAS future-combat-aircraft programme, with a German official signalling agreement on how parts of it — the fighter data links and "combat cloud" software — would continue, even as France watches Germany build Europe's leading conventional army. The next flashpoint is the joint future tank meant to replace the Leclerc and Leopard 2. Two joint declarations on defence and the wider relationship are expected on 17 July.

Industry Impact

The immediate ACS relevance is second-order but strategically important: a Franco-German push to protect European industry and rebuild defence-industrial capacity signals demand for advanced structural adhesives, coatings and sealants in aerospace, defence and rail programmes. It also shapes the policy environment — energy, industrial subsidies and trade protection — that determines whether European chemical and manufacturing production stays viable. Track the 17 July declarations for concrete industrial and energy commitments that could underpin European end-market demand.

Politico Europe | Anadolu Agency | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Arab News | Le Dauphine Libere

item.title: Eni CEO Descalzi told parliament that Europe has effectively told chemical producers to leave and that 20% of the industry has closed, while Japan weighs restoring a naphtha reserve after Middle East risk caused paint and solvent shortages.
item.description:
These two items frame the same structural squeeze from opposite ends. Descalzi's language was unusually blunt for an energy CEO — Europe has "done everything to destroy the chemical industry" — and he backed it with a hard number: a fifth of Europe's chemical capacity has shut. His own firm, he said, absorbed losses and pivoted into biochemistry without state help and without a single redundancy. Japan's response to the same input insecurity is pre-emptive: Tokyo is considering rebuilding a strategic naphtha reserve because shortages of paints and solvents are already hitting housing and construction, with ~40% of naphtha imported from the Middle East and much domestic output made from regional crude. Separately, the IEA confirmed the EU Methane Regulation could cut EU refinery runs and shrink the tradable-crude pool by over 50% from January 2027 — another self-inflicted pressure on European feedstock security.

Industry Impact

This is the most directly ACS-relevant cluster in the alert. Naphtha and solvents are foundational to coatings and adhesives, and a paint/solvent shortage acute enough to prompt Japanese stockpiling is a live availability warning for the whole sector. Descalzi's "20% closed" figure quantifies the erosion of Europe's chemical base that ACS producers depend on for local supply. Model naphtha and solvent security explicitly, watch the EU Methane Regulation's January 2027 bite on refinery output, and treat European feedstock availability — not just price — as a strategic risk.

Il Sole 24 Ore | The Nation | MarketScreener | FuelsEurope

item.title: A Fraunhofer study projects up to 726,000 European automotive job losses by 2040, VW's board rejected CEO Blume's plan to close four plants, and Merz said he would not oppose Chinese carmakers taking over struggling German factories.
item.description:
The pressure that produced VW's 50,000-job warning in the last alert has now hit an inflection. Fraunhofer quantifies the long-run risk at 726,000 European jobs by 2040 (375,000 by 2030), with BMW, Porsche and VW all running savings programmes. But VW's supervisory board refused to back Blume's plan to close four plants and cut a further 50,000 jobs, opting instead for a vaguer "Future Plan" to halve the model line-up, cut complexity 75% and trim capacity to 9m vehicles. Into that vacuum steps a striking political shift: Merz said he would not object to Chinese manufacturers taking over idle German plants — an emergency fix, not a cure — while Saxony's economy minister wants higher China car tariffs to make a Zwickau joint venture pay. Baden-Württemberg has set up a task force as Mercedes and Porsche cut jobs and shift work to Hungary.

Industry Impact

Automotive is a core ACS end-market — structural adhesives, coatings and sealants ride on European vehicle output — so a secular shrinkage of German production directly erodes demand. Chinese takeovers of German plants could preserve volume but reshuffle the supplier base toward Chinese-qualified materials, a competitive threat to incumbent ACS suppliers. Watch which plants survive and under whose ownership, and position early to qualify into any Chinese-run European lines rather than assuming legacy specifications hold.

Die Zeit | The Association of European Vehicle Logistics | Lianhe Zaobao | Commercial Times | MarketScreener

item.title: Standard Chartered cut its 2026 global growth forecast to 3%, the IMF put UK growth at just 1% as May GDP crept up 0.1%, and the Bank of Korea raised rates to 2.75% — its first hike since 2023 — as the Middle East conflict feeds inflation.
item.description:
Three separate data points describe one story: the war is now visible in the macro numbers. Standard Chartered attributed its downgrade from 3.4% squarely to the Middle East conflict, and warned that AI-investment demand flattered H1 while underlying growth was moderate. The IMF's UK read is consistent — 1% growth in 2026, recovering to 1.3% in 2027 as the energy shock fades, alongside a warning to incoming PM Andy Burnham to avoid spending hikes, price caps or broad subsidies. Most striking is South Korea: the Bank of Korea's first rate rise in over three years is an explicit response to war-driven inflation and high household debt, and markets recoiled, with the KOSPI falling more than 6% intraday and triggering a trading halt amid an AI-chip sell-off. Central banks are being pushed toward tightening precisely as growth slows.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers this is a demand-and-cost squeeze. Slower global growth and downgraded construction and manufacturing activity mean softer end-market volumes, while war-driven inflation keeps input and energy costs elevated. Rate hikes like Korea's raise financing costs and can cool the construction demand that underpins coatings and sealants. Plan for a stagflation-lite H2 — weaker volumes and sticky costs together — and prioritise pricing discipline and working-capital efficiency over volume-led growth assumptions.

Commercial Times | Dünya Gazetesi | MarketScreener | AP | MarketScreener

item.title: A revised Senate bill would impose 100% tariffs on China, India, Azerbaijan, Hungary and Slovakia for buying Russian oil while exempting 15 European gas importers, keeping alive a secondary-sanctions threat aimed at the two largest Asian economies.
item.description:
The bill carries over from the last alert but the framing has sharpened. The 100% rate is already a climb-down from an earlier 500% draft, and the carve-out for 15 European buyers — justified on the grounds that Russian gas is a small share of their supply and is being phased out — exposes the measure to charges of selectivity. India has reason to stay measured: Washington imposed a 25% India tariff over Russian crude last year, then reversed it in February, suggesting the threat is a negotiating lever as much as a firm policy. Still, if enacted, it would collide directly with the Brazil action and the China disputes to produce a dense, overlapping tariff landscape. China has already rejected the approach as illegal.

Industry Impact

A 100% tariff on China and India would be a severe shock to global chemical trade, given both are major producers and consumers of chemical intermediates and finished goods. Even as a threat, it raises planning uncertainty for anyone with China- or India-linked supply. The exemption logic also matters: it shows energy-import dependence is now a tariff trigger, so exposure maps should include not just where inputs are made but the energy sources behind them. Watch the vote path closely and keep contingency sourcing for China/India-dependent lines.

The Times of India

item.title: The IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook warns that fully enforcing China's rare-earth export controls could put USD 6.5tn of production outside China at risk — nearly half in Europe and the US — with graphite curbs threatening a further USD 300bn.
item.description:
The report reframes what had been a Japan-specific story in the last alert into a systemic, quantified risk. China controls more than 90% of processed graphite and dominates most metal value chains for solar, wind, batteries and electronics. The IEA models what happens if Beijing's controls — already applied to seven heavy rare earths in April 2025 and now proposed for foreign products containing Chinese materials — are fully enforced: energy, defence, high-tech and automotive supply chains face severe disruption. Other producers are following the same playbook, with cobalt quotas in the DRC and measures on lithium in Zimbabwe and graphite in Mozambique, so concentration risk is spreading rather than diversifying. The finding lands as the EU stands up a crisis task force ahead of an October expiry of a temporary rare-earth arrangement (see other insight in this alert).

Industry Impact

Rare earths and graphite are not core ACS inputs, but the exposure is indirect and real: customer industries — automotive, electronics, batteries, defence — sit squarely in the USD 6.5tn at risk, so a full Chinese clampdown would hit demand for adhesives, coatings and sealants used in those sectors. It also signals that mineral-based export controls are becoming a routine geopolitical weapon, a template that could extend to chemical intermediates. Track downstream customer exposure and treat supply concentration as a demand-side as well as a cost-side risk.

Nikkei Asian Review | Anadolu Agency | Cnyes.com

item.title: Washington will impose 25% duties on thousands of Brazilian goods from 22 July — its first action under a new Section 301 strategy — prompting Brazil to threaten reciprocal tariffs and a WTO challenge weeks before its October election.
item.description:
This is a fresh escalation in a different theatre from the Russian-energy and China disputes. The duties cover sugar, apparel, paper, steel, wood, machinery and corn ethanol, with beef and coffee exempted to spare US consumers. The USTR grounded the action in alleged unfair practices spanning electronic payments — Brazil's Pix instant-payment system is a specific target — ethanol, intellectual property, anti-corruption enforcement and environmental protection. Secretary of State Rubio framed it bluntly, saying Trump ordered the tariff because Lula "has not negotiated in good faith". Brasília condemned the move, threatened immediate retaliation and signalled it would escalate to the WTO, hardening a rift that now overshadows Brazil's presidential race. Because this is the debut of the Section 301 template, it matters beyond Brazil: it is the mechanism Washington can now replicate against other trading partners.

Industry Impact

Direct ACS exposure to Brazil is modest, but the precedent is the point: a reusable Section 301 tariff engine raises the probability of sudden, country-specific duties on chemical inputs and finished goods elsewhere. Steel and machinery duties feed into construction and manufacturing costs across the Americas, and Brazilian retaliation could disrupt US chemical and agricultural exports. Treat this as a signal to map tariff-exposure scenarios by country, not just by product, and to keep sourcing flexibility for inputs that could be caught in a widening tariff net.

Al Jazeera | Financial Times | Anadolu Agency | ABC.es

item.title: US strikes expanded to targets near Tehran and disabled a ship trying to break the Hormuz blockade, Iran retaliated against Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait, and oil rose a fourth day before easing as Goldman warned Brent could top USD 110.
item.description:
The delta since the last alert is geographic and vertical escalation. Strikes that had focused on coastal defences now reach northern Iran near Tehran, CENTCOM reported dozens of targets hit over seven hours, and for the first time the US forcibly disabled a vessel attempting to run the blockade. Iran answered by firing missiles and drones at US allies across the Gulf, widening the conflict beyond the strait itself. Markets are ambivalent: crude rose a fourth session on the strikes, then gave back gains on profit-taking, leaving Brent near USD 84.5. The forward risk is asymmetric — Goldman Sachs sees Brent above USD 110 by Q4 if Gulf exports stay obstructed, while the IEA's Fatih Birol warned the global economy faces new strain if Hormuz, which carried a fifth of world oil and gas, is not reopened within weeks.

Industry Impact

For chemical and ACS producers the transmission is through feedstock and freight, not direct exposure. Crude and naphtha set the cost base for adhesives, coatings and sealants, and the reserve buffer that has capped prices is finite — OECD countries have already injected roughly 400 million barrels. Hormuz traffic has thinned, lengthening delivery times and lifting tanker and insurance costs on Gulf-routed petrochemical and base-oil cargoes. Plan H2 for both input-cost inflation and the tail risk of a genuine supply break, and keep Gulf-dependent supply under active stress-testing.

AP | The Guardian | Commercial Times | Lianhe Zaobao | Dünya Gazetesi | Le Figaro

item.title: MIA Digest: The US-Iran war widened toward Tehran and the Gulf as oil wavered near USD 85; Washington opened a 25% tariff front on Brazil; the IEA flagged USD 6.5tn at risk from China's rare-earth curbs; and StanChart cut 2026 global growth to 3%.
item.description:
• Iran war: US strikes reached near Tehran and disabled a blockade-running ship, Iran hit Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait, and oil rose a fourth day before easing near USD 85 as Goldman warned Brent could top USD 110.
  • New tariff front: Washington will hit most Brazilian imports with 25% duties from 22 July — its first Section 301 action — and Brazil threatened reciprocal tariffs and a WTO challenge.
  • Critical minerals: the IEA warned that fully enforcing China's rare-earth export controls could put USD 6.5tn of production outside China at risk, with graphite curbs threatening a further USD 300bn.
  • Growth and rates: Standard Chartered cut 2026 global growth to 3%, the IMF put UK growth at 1%, and the Bank of Korea raised rates to 2.75% — its first hike since 2023 — as war-driven inflation spreads.
  • European chemicals: Eni's CEO said the EU is 'destroying' the chemical industry with 20% already closed, while Japan weighed a naphtha reserve after paint and solvent shortages.
